name: Patellofemoral Pain
summary: Patellofemoral pain (PFP) is pain at the front of the knee, around or behind the kneecap (patella), that is made worse by loading the joint between the kneecap and the thigh bone, for example when squatting, climbing stairs, running or sitting for a long time. It is common in active young adults, especially women and runners, and in adolescents.

looksLike: Diffuse pain at the front of the knee, often hard to point to with one finger.
Pain with stairs (especially going down), squatting, running, jumping, kneeling, and long periods of sitting with bent knees (the moviegoer sign).
Sometimes grinding or clicking without pain, which is common and not by itself a problem.
Usually no major swelling, no locking, and no true giving way. If these are present, consider other diagnoses.
redFlags: Adolescent with knee pain, limp and limited or painful hip rotation
Hot, red, swollen knee with fever
Fall or injury with immediate swelling, inability to bear weight or a visible deformity
Constant night pain, weight loss, a bony lump
firstSteps: Initial approach: education, load management and exercise therapy.
Justifying findings: anterior knee pain, typical triggers, positive squat or step-down, no flags.
Priority: build knee and hip strength and load tolerance.

assess: Observe standing alignment, foot posture and muscle bulk. Alignment findings are not reliable by themselves for diagnosis.
Watch functional tasks: double-leg squat, single-leg squat and step-down. Note pain, trunk and hip control and knee movement.
Palpate the patellar edges, patellar tendon, quadriceps tendon and fat pad.
Range of movement, effusion check, ligament and meniscal tests to exclude other causes.
Strength of quadriceps, hip abductors, extensors and external rotators.
Flexibility: quadriceps, hamstrings, calf, and the iliotibial band region.

blocks.text: **Patellofemoral pain (PFP)** is pain at the front of the knee, around or behind the kneecap (patella), that is made worse by loading the joint between the kneecap and the thigh bone, for example when squatting, climbing stairs, running or sitting for a long time. It is common in active young adults, especially women and runners, and in adolescents [Ref - to verify].

The cause is not fully understood. Likely contributors include a sudden rise in activity load, reduced capacity of the thigh and hip muscles, and the way the knee and hip are used in activity. Older explanations such as simple kneecap mistracking or poor alignment as the only cause are not well supported [Ref - to verify]. Pain is real, and most people improve with exercise-based care, although a large share still have symptoms years later [Ref - to verify].
PFP is a clinical diagnosis. It is made when other knee problems have been reasonably excluded.

items: Diffuse pain at the front of the knee, often hard to point to with one finger.
Pain with stairs (especially going down), squatting, running, jumping, kneeling, and long periods of sitting with bent knees (the moviegoer sign).
Sometimes grinding or clicking without pain, which is common and not by itself a problem.
Usually no major swelling, no locking, and no true giving way. If these are present, consider other diagnoses.

blocks.text: **Diagnostic features used in consensus statements:** anterior knee pain around or behind the patella, provoked by at least one of squatting, stair use, prolonged sitting, running, hopping or jumping, and reproduced by squatting, a step-down or palpation of the patellar edges, with other conditions excluded [Ref - to verify exact wording].

rows: Where is the pain: around or behind the kneecap, or below it?
Around or behind supports PFP; just below suggests the patellar tendon
What activities provoke it? Stairs, squats, running, sitting?
Has your training or activity changed recently?
Load increase is a common trigger
Does it swell, lock or give way?
Has the kneecap ever slipped out?
Any hip or groin pain, or a limp (especially in a teenager)?
Hip problem referred to the knee
Any fever, night pain, constant pain?
What do you want to do again?

blocks.text: Honest note: many classic patellar tests (compression, grind, Q-angle) have poor accuracy and are not recommended as stand-alone diagnostic tests [Ref - to verify]. Functional provocation tests are more useful for diagnosis and for monitoring.
E1. Single-leg squat or step-down test

rows: Reproduce the familiar pain in a loaded, weight-bearing position and observe movement control
Standing on the painful leg, hands on hips or free, facing a mirror if possible
Slowly squat on one leg to about 45 to 60 degrees of knee bend, or step down from a low step and tap the heel lightly. Repeat several times
Reproduction of the familiar anterior knee pain
PFP, particularly when the double-leg squat is also painful
Note if the trunk leans, the pelvis drops or the knee moves inward. These are observations, not proof of cause
Pain only shows that the joint is irritable. Visual movement ratings vary between observers [Ref - to verify]
Use the test as a baseline for monitoring treatment

blocks.text: E2. Palpation of patellar edges
Press gently along the medial and lateral edges of the patella with the knee relaxed. **Positive:** tenderness that reproduces the familiar pain. Tenderness is common and not specific.
E3. Patellar apprehension (Fairbank) test

rows: Supine, knee bent to about 20 to 30 degrees and relaxed
The patient shows apprehension, contracts the quadriceps or resists
If positive, use the instability pathway and consider medical review

blocks.text: E4. Patellar tendon and fat pad tests

Pain on palpation of the inferior pole of the patella and on a single-leg decline squat suggests patellar tendinopathy. Pain at the front of the knee with passive full extension or tenderness on both sides of the patellar tendon suggests fat pad irritation.
E5. Outcome measures
Anterior Knee Pain Scale (Kujala), a 0 to 10 pain scale, and the pain level during a single-leg squat or step-down [Ref - to verify].

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.
Adolescent with a limp or hip signs? **Yes:** hip examination and urgent referral if needed.
Anterior knee pain around the patella with typical triggers and a positive squat or step-down test, and no locking, major swelling or injury? **Yes:** working diagnosis is patellofemoral pain.
Another condition fits better (tendinopathy, instability, meniscal)? Use that pathway.
Start exercise therapy with education and load management.
If no improvement after a suitable trial, review the diagnosis and consider medical opinion.

rows: Soft-tissue work (quadriceps, iliotibial band region, calf)
Short-term comfort and ease of exercise
Short-term pain relief in some patients [Ref - to verify]
Stiff painful patella with limited glide
Supine, gentle medial, lateral and superior glides

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** education and exercise. Manual therapy alone is not enough. Do not claim to correct kneecap tracking or realign the patella through manual techniques. Where manual therapy is used, combine it with exercise [Ref - to verify].

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

blocks.text: **Principle:** consensus statements place exercise therapy, combining knee and hip exercises, as the first-line treatment, often for at least 3 months, together with education and load management [Ref - to verify]. The aim is to increase the capacity of the knee to take load.

rows: Isometric quadriceps hold (wall sit at shallow angle, or seated knee extension hold)
Hold with knee bent about 45 to 60 degrees
Pain above 5 out of 10 or lasting into the next day
Lying on the side, lift the top leg
Clam or banded hip external rotation
As in Vol 4 Ch 1; add load
Graded walk to run, then volume and speed

blocks.text: **Symptom rule:** pain up to about 3 to 4 out of 10 during exercise that settles within 24 hours is acceptable [Ref - to verify]. Avoid long periods of the most painful activity during the early weeks, but do not stop activity altogether.

**Load management:** reduce, rather than stop, painful activity. For runners, lower weekly volume or intensity, shorten the stride length slightly or raise the step rate a little (about 5 to 10 percent) in selected cases, then rebuild gradually [Ref - to verify].
**Adjuncts:**

rows: Short-term pain relief to allow exercise
Evidence mixed; use only if it helps in the session [Ref - to verify]
Short-term benefit in some patients, especially with flat or pronated feet
Therapeutic ultrasound, laser, electrical stimulation as a routine treatment
Weak or no added benefit [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: Injections and surgery are rarely needed for PFP and are medical decisions.

**Middle:** progress knee and hip strengthening and function, build tolerance to stairs, squats and sport.

blocks.text: **Case:** A 24-year-old recreational runner has 8 weeks of pain around the front of the right knee after increasing weekly distance. It is worse on stairs downward and after sitting. No swelling, locking or giving way. Squat and step-down reproduce the pain. Hip abduction strength is reduced. Hip examination is normal.

**Working diagnosis:** patellofemoral pain. **Plan:** education, reduce running volume by about half, begin isometrics, then knee and hip strengthening, add taping if it helps, graded return to running, reassess every 2 weeks.
**Questions and answers**

items: Why are grind and compression tests not enough? They have poor accuracy and many pain-free knees are tender or noisy, so functional tests and history are more useful [Ref - to verify].
Why do we avoid saying the kneecap is out of place? The tracking explanation is not well supported and can increase fear of movement.
A 14-year-old has knee pain and a limp. What do you check? The hip. Limited painful hip rotation needs urgent referral to exclude a slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
Why strengthen the hip as well as the knee? Consensus statements recommend combined knee and hip exercise, because it may give better pain relief than knee exercise alone [Ref - to verify].
The knee suddenly locks and will not straighten. What now? Suspect a mechanical block, refer for orthopaedic review.
**Initial approach:** education, load management and exercise therapy.
**Justifying findings:** anterior knee pain, typical triggers, positive squat or step-down, no flags.
**Priority:** build knee and hip strength and load tolerance.
**Manual therapy:** minor adjunct.
**Exercise:** isometrics, then knee and hip strengthening, then functional and sport drills.
**Modalities:** limited role.
**Tell the patient:** this is common, treatable and not a sign of damage; recovery can take months.
**Avoid:** complete rest, fear-based explanations, relying on passive treatments.
**Measure:** squat pain, Kujala, strength.
**If no improvement:** review the diagnosis and consider specialist opinion.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** pain controlled, function and sport restored, maintenance plan.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** no injury, no locking, no instability.

items: **Can be tested:** whether combined knee and hip exercise improves pain and function; whether taping or orthoses add benefit.
**Hypotheses:** that muscle capacity and load management reduce joint stress; that hip strength influences knee loading.
**Future questions:** best exercise type, dose and duration; why some patients stay symptomatic.

blocks.text: Evidence not graded until references are verified.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Explain PFP in plain language without blaming kneecap tracking.
Run a single-leg squat or step-down test and use it as a baseline.
Recognise adolescent hip referral and other urgent causes.
Build a knee and hip exercise program with clear progression.
